newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Concerns raised over proposed SAfrica tax holidays.
newsitem.headline: Concerns raised over proposed SAfrica tax holidays.

text.p: The planned introduction of tax holidays to attract investment and create jobs could be far more complicated than appears at face value and would have to be carefully monitored.

This was the message to emerge at the end of a two-day hearing by the parliamentary finance committee into the Revenue Laws Amendment Bill which aims to introduce changes to the country's tax system -- among them tax holidays.
The changes were announced in government's macro-economic strategy document on June 14.
The Trade and Industry Department said tax holidays were expected to result in a "fiscal transfer" of two billion rand to companies by 1999, or 10 percent of present corporate tax.
This was less than what was paid out under former incentive schemes such as the general export incentive scheme (GEIS) and was seen as a more efficient means of promoting investment.
A South African Chamber of Business delegation warned, however, that government was "dealing with complex legislation that is going to have ramifications...

"This committee will need to review this legislation from time to time and organised business has to look at the practical applications...we are sure that there will be many amendments needed as it is put into practice."

It was particularly concerned that tax holidays could disadvantage existing companies and about whether government had the administrative capacity to ensure that there were "no unintended consequences".
The delegation also had several technical problems with the bill.
For their part, committee members were more concerned about the sustainability of enterprises set up with the help of tax holidays once the incentives expired.

Some of them said they had vivid memories of industries set up in the former black homelands under the apartheid era with the help of similar incentives, only to "get up and go" once the incentives ran out.

The envisaged tax holidays will provide a maximum of six years tax exemption as long as new projects meet certain criteria on increasing competitiveness, job creation and adding to the manufacturing base in certain areas.

Alan Hirsch, Trade and Industry Department chief director for industry and technology, said that a number of alternatives had been considered and "the reason that we preferred tax holidays was...that it is performance based.
"We will only reward a company that is actually successful," he said, adding that it would be closely monitored to ensure long-term viability.
The committee, which can technically only accept or reject the "money" bill, will finalise its report next week
